items.title: Rashied Ali and Henry Grimes interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 30, 2009
items.q: And so George Wein made a deal with us actually to make us a part of his festival... George Wein got them a place and advertised it on his Newport stuff and got avant garde people a venue, a couple of venues, for them to play on his festival as well.

ctx.x: You know you were talking the other day, I guess yesterday, about the effort that you made, both of you, back a number of years ago to get free or avant garde jazz on some of these festivals, that they weren’t presenting that spectrum of the music. And in the last year or so I went to a big jazz convention and the people that promote Dixieland music, or very early, were complaining about the same thing. And it’s like they’re leaving out the ends of the music. Do you agree with that? And can you tell me about —

Well back, like in the 70s, like the early part of the 70s, I don’t know too much about the Dixieland but probably all even Dixieland and avant garde now, but not now, not so much now, because the avant garde is really popular in Europe. And I mean you know we get like huge crowds in Europe with this stuff. And it’s festivals attracts a lot of people from all around. But actually it really got a hold there more or less more so than here. In fact, most of the European players that play jazz are into avant garde…

then even some of the main jazz clubs will hire like the really name avant garde players like Cecil Taylor or Ornette Coleman and sometimes I even get a shot at it too, because I’m sort of like an old-timer now. And so we get to play in a lot of the major clubs here now. But in the 70s it wasn’t about to be had, you know. We were hurting for places to play, we were hurting for recording companies to record us, so we were forced to start our own kind of venues. We went into like into loft situations in New York…
